source.title: U-shaped and Inverted-U Scaling behind Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports model-compute scaling results on LLM benchmark questions, extending the double-descent-like pattern to difficulty-stratified downstream-task performance. It does not reproduce the original test-error/interpolation-threshold experiment.
record.gate_note: The study measures performance across model training compute, stratifies questions by difficulty, and reports scaling trends. It does not sweep epochs or training-sample size. The discussion of deep double descent and its bias-variance explanation cites prior work rather than testing those mechanisms here. The study also reports accuracy trends and compares them with its TC Brier Score trends.
record.test_reason: The study does not test V1 or any other version. It tracks downstream benchmark scores of 56 pretrained LLMs from many families against log training compute, which mixes parameters and tokens. Its question-difficulty groups are defined using the scores of the same sub-threshold models. Its main results are an inverted-U for easy questions and a U-shape for hard ones. No interpolation threshold is identified, model size is not isolated, and the measure is not test error versus capacity around fitting the training set. The authors link the easy-question curve to deep double descent only by analogy (Sec. 3.1) and explain it with cited bias-variance arguments. The finding is a related but different construct, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors report U-shaped scaling for hard questions and inverted-U then improvement for easy questions on six emergent multiple-choice tasks, propose this as a possible cause of emergence, and use it in the Slice-and-Sandwich forecast. They acknowledge that not all emergent tasks may show the pattern clearly. The link to deep double descent is stated as consistency or analogy, not tested.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates LLM benchmark performance across log training compute and difficulty groups using TC Brier Score and accuracy. It does not reproduce the original test-error experiment around the interpolation threshold or isolate parameter-count scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed pattern varies with question difficulty, dataset, and metric. The supplementary text reports that Hindu knowledge and conceptual combinations have the opposite easy/hard assignment, analogical similarity has a mild hard-group U shape and no easiest-group reversion before the emergence threshold, and hard-group U-shaped scaling is mitigated when measured by accuracy instead of TC Brier Score.

fits_no_version.finding: On difficulty-stratified LLM benchmarks, easiest-question TC Brier Score and accuracy rise, fall, then rise again with log training compute (MMLU, arithmetic, Persian-QA). The analogical similarity easiest group does not revert before the emergence threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream LLM performance on post-hoc easy question subsets scales non-monotonically (inverted-U then improvement) with training compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Hard questions show U-shaped TC Brier scaling. Hindu knowledge and conceptual combinations show U-shaped easy groups and inverted-U hard groups. Under accuracy, hard groups stagnate near zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The direction of difficulty-stratified inverse scaling varies by task and metric.

record.problems: The paper reports qualitative curves without uncertainty estimates. Its log-compute comparison does not isolate parameter count from training tokens, and it does not identify a training-set interpolation threshold. The conclusions depend on the proposed TC Brier Score; the paper reports that hard-group curves are less clear with accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: The individual-question probability examples in Supplementary Tables A3 and A4 are illustrative rather than aggregate scaling-curve measurements and are not separately extracted. Other supplementary analyses of the forecasting pipeline are omitted because they do not add a distinct result on the claim's scaling pattern.

untested.parts: Test error versus model size; a peak at the interpolation threshold; isolation of parameter count from training tokens and model family.

missing.what: Pythia-70m/160m/1b, trained on the same data so only parameter count varies, show inverted-U TC Brier on six hand-picked easiest MMLU questions. This is the closest to a size-only axis, but the questions are illustrative and selected.

Non-emergent tasks (abstract narrative understanding, ARC, HellaSwag) show no inverted-U for easy groups. Most groups improve steadily, and the easiest and hardest groups of ARC and HellaSwag are flat.
Under the un-conditionalized TC Brier Score, arithmetic and Persian-QA show no inverse scaling on any interval, so the pattern depends on the metric.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T3 and V1 labels are rejected. The compute axis conflates N and D across many families, and no interpolation threshold exists. The difficulty grouping is computed from the same sub-threshold models whose curves are then plotted, a selection likely to produce non-monotone curves by regression to the mean; the paper has no control for this. There are no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure test error around the training-set interpolation threshold or isolate model parameter count from training compute. It studies downstream benchmark performance over model log compute, mainly by question-difficulty group.
No sweep over training epochs or time.
No change in training-sample count near an interpolation threshold.
No test of risk versus capacity across model classes or at an interpolation point; the paper discusses deep double descent from prior work.
No single effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak locations across axes.
No experiments on label noise, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameter number.

rows.subject: LLMs (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: diverse training compute; 56 LLMs are reported for the MMLU evaluation
rows.operation_detail: Compared difficulty-grouped benchmark performance across model log compute.
rows.measure: TC Brier Score (higher indicates higher performance)
rows.value: Performance first increases, then worsens, followed by a second ascent; the paper describes this as inverted-U scaling followed by steady improvement.
rows.note: The reported performance pattern corresponds to a fall-rise-fall pattern in loss, but the study does not measure test error at an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: This is the MMLU easiest-group TC Brier curve against log compute (N×D) across heterogeneous model families. There is no interpolation threshold or size-only axis, so it does not measure V1's model-wise test-error peak.

rows.value: The paper reports clear inverted-U scaling for the easiest group, followed by steady improvement.
rows.note: The paper describes this result jointly for the three datasets.
rows.check: Accuracy for the easiest groups is inverted-U then improving. Here too the difficulty groups are defined by the sub-threshold models' accuracy, which is a selection that can by itself produce non-monotone curves. It is not a V1 measure.

conditions.value: hard groups, including the hardest groups

rows.value: Hard groups do not show a clear U-shaped scaling pattern; the hardest groups stagnate after the initial performance drop at near-zero accuracy, lower than random guess.
rows.note: This contrasts with the TC Brier Score results for hard questions; the authors say accuracy does not capture changes in confidence.
rows.check: Hard-group accuracy stagnates near zero. It bears on the study's U-shaped hard-question claim, not on V1.
